name: Restaurant Bofinger
short_description: Belle Epoque Alsatian brasserie founded in 1864, said to be the first establishment in Paris to serve draught beer, crowned by a stained-glass dome.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Paris's oldest Alsatian brasserie, famed for its choucroute and Belle Epoque interior — strong Food & Culinary Culture and Historic Architecture candidate.

name: Marché Bastille
short_description: Open-air food market stretching along Boulevard Richard-Lenoir on Thursdays and Sundays, one of the largest in Paris with the Colonne de Juillet as its backdrop.

_pipeline.address: Boulevard Richard-Lenoir (between Rue Amelot and Rue Saint-Sabin), 75011 Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: One of the biggest open-air markets in central Paris, popular with both locals and tourists for produce, seafood and flowers.

name: Cour Damoye
short_description: Private cobbled passage off the Place de la Bastille, opened in 1780 on the old Saint-Antoine glacis and once filled with wagon repair and faubourg craft workshops.

_pipeline.address: 12 Place de la Bastille to 12 Rue Daval, 75011 Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Hidden artisan courtyard moments from the Bastille traffic — strong Hidden History and Art & Street Culture candidate.

name: Barrio Latino
short_description: Multi-level Cuban-themed bar, restaurant and dance club that opened near Opéra Bastille in 1999 and was rebranded as Pachamama at the same address.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Once a four-floor Latin nightlife landmark by the Bastille, now operating as Pachamama; useful for nightlife and Faubourg Saint-Antoine context.

name: Passage du Chantier
short_description: Cobbled passageway off Rue du Faubourg Saint-Antoine that still houses some of the last cabinetmaker and furniture workshops of the historic faubourg.

discovery_sources: Un jour de plus à Paris
_pipeline.discovery_notes: A surviving fragment of the faubourg's 17th-century furniture trade, lined with active ateliers — strong candidate for Hidden History and Shopping & Markets.

name: Quinze-Vingts National Ophthalmology Hospital
short_description: National eye hospital founded in 1260 by Louis IX as a hospice for 300 blind Parisians, relocated in 1779 to the former Black Musketeers barracks on Rue de Charenton.
name_variations: Centre Hospitalier National d'Ophtalmologie des Quinze-Vingts

_pipeline.discovery_notes: One of the oldest continually operating hospitals in Europe and home to the Vision Institute — bridges Hidden History, Religious & Spiritual Sites and Science & Innovation.

name: Viaduc des Arts
short_description: Mid-19th-century railway viaduct converted in the 1990s into a row of artisan workshops in glass, jewellery and furniture, beneath the elevated Promenade Plantee.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Iconic Paris adaptive-reuse project pairing crafts and a green roof — strong Modern & Contemporary Design and Shopping & Markets candidate.

name: Roger-Viollet Photo Agency
short_description: Photographic agency founded in 1938 by Hélène Roger-Viollet that holds more than two million images covering 150 years of Parisian and world history.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: A pillar of Paris photographic memory, now an archive and gallery on the Left Bank — fits Art & Street Culture and Literary & Film Locations adjacency.

name: George Sand's House (31 Rue de Seine)
short_description: Saint-Germain townhouse where novelist George Sand lived in 1831; the same building later hosted Raymond Duncan's Akademia from 1929 to 1966.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: A façade-only literary stop on Rick Steves' Left Bank walk, marking Sand's bohemian Paris years — Literary & Film Locations.

name: Café la Palette
short_description: Artist-favoured Left Bank café opened in 1902 next to the École des Beaux-Arts, with a Belle Epoque storefront and 1930s ceramic interior listed as a historic monument since 1984.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Cézanne, Picasso and Hemingway-era hangout still drawing artists and tourists — Food & Culinary Culture plus Art & Street Culture.

name: Richard Wagner's House (14 Rue Jacob)
short_description: Saint-Germain residence where composer Richard Wagner lived from October 1841 to April 1842 and wrote the overture to The Flying Dutchman, marked today by a commemorative plaque.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: A Music Heritage façade stop tied to the genesis of The Flying Dutchman; plaque unveiled by the Paris Wagner Circle in 2000.

name: Palais Abbatial de Saint-Germain-des-Prés
short_description: Brick-and-stone abbatial palace built in 1586 for Cardinal Charles de Bourbon, an early Parisian example of the style that would later define Place Dauphine and Place des Vosges.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Listed historic monument since 1959 and a precursor to Henri IV's Place Royale brick-and-stone vernacular — Historic Architecture and Religious & Spiritual Sites.

name: Hôtel de Crillon
short_description: Five-star Rosewood-managed palace hotel in a 1758 Ange-Jacques Gabriel building where Benjamin Franklin signed the 1778 Franco-American treaty recognising US independence.
name_variations: Hotel de Crillon, A Rosewood Hotel

_pipeline.discovery_notes: One of two Gabriel palaces fronting the Concorde, with a documented role in the Franco-American alliance — Historic Architecture, Hidden History and War & Revolution.
